christadelphian.trinity:
Christadelphians hold that God is one, and that this one God is the Father. Jesus is the Son of God, born of Mary through a miracle of God's power, and is truly the Lord and Savior, but he is not himself God. The Holy Spirit is understood as the power of God, by which he acts and inspires, and not a separate person of the Godhead.

For Christadelphians this is simply what the Bible says, and they regard the Trinity as a later doctrine developed through Greek philosophy. Their use of the phrase God is one is meant to keep faith close to the wording of Scripture. Other Christians who hold the Trinity generally disagree, and Christadelphians see this as one of the main differences between themselves and the larger churches.
christadelphian.preexistence_of_christ:
Christadelphians teach that Jesus did not exist as a person before his birth. He existed beforehand in the plan and purpose of God, and the promises of a coming Messiah point toward him, but he came into being when he was conceived and born of Mary.

This matters to them because they hold that Jesus shared our human nature completely, and was tempted as we are, yet never sinned. Because of that, they say, he can truly stand in our place and be our representative before God. They read passages that speak of Christ before all things as describing what was in God's purpose. Christians who teach that Christ is the eternal Son understand these passages differently.
christadelphian.soul_sleep:
Christadelphians speak of the sleep of the dead. They teach that human beings do not have an immortal soul that lives on after death. At death a person is entirely dead, unconscious, and waits in the grave until the resurrection.

The hope is therefore resurrection and judgment when Christ returns, and not a heaven or hell immediately after dying. Those judged faithful are raised to eternal life in the kingdom of God on a renewed earth, and the rest do not live again to suffer forever. Christadelphians support this from Scripture passages which liken death to sleep. It differs from teaching that the soul goes at once to be with the Lord, and Christadelphians know it seems unusual to many other believers.
